analysis.one_liner: Caps monthly out-of-pocket prescription drug costs at $250 per person in most health plans.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it sat in a House subcommittee until the two-year Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would limit what people pay out of pocket for prescription drugs to $250 a month for an individual and $500 for a family, in both Affordable Care Act marketplace plans and employer group health plans, starting with plans in 2025, with the cap rising with medical inflation afterward. It was introduced in November 2023, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then its Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 118th Congress ended. [S2] [S3] [S5]
analysis.who_benefits: People who take expensive prescription drugs, especially patients on high-cost specialty medications whose monthly out-of-pocket costs currently exceed $250, along with families whose combined drug costs exceed $500 a month. [S3]

how_it_helps.text: For plan years beginning in 2025, an enrollee's total cost-sharing for prescription drugs covered by a qualified health plan could not exceed $250 per month per individual or $500 per month per family. [S3]
The cap also applies to employer group health plans, because the bill ties the limits in the Public Health Service Act to the same ACA provision. [S3]
For 2026 and later years, the $250/$500 amounts rise each year with the medical care component of the Consumer Price Index, so the protection does not erode with inflation. [S3]
The bill takes effect for plans beginning after December 31, 2024. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers sponsoring group plans would absorb the cost of drug charges above the cap, which would likely flow back into higher premiums; drug makers could keep prices high because patients would no longer face the full cost at the pharmacy counter. [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Insurers, employers, and all premium payers

drawbacks.text: The cap limits what patients pay but not what drugs cost, so insurers and employers pick up charges above $250 a month, and those costs would likely come back to households as higher premiums across all plans. [S3]

Because patients would pay the same out of pocket regardless of which drug they take, the cap weakens price sensitivity at the pharmacy and could reduce pressure on drug makers to keep prices in check. [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly one in twenty enrollees with out-of-pocket drug costs above $250 a month, the bill is a direct, meaningful benefit. But it works by having insurers and employers absorb the excess rather than by lowering drug prices themselves, so the savings partly resurface as higher premiums for everyone, and it could ease pressure on manufacturers' pricing. It is a real protection for a narrow group, paid for broadly.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Health Subcommittee, and it stayed there without a hearing or vote until the Congress ended in January 2025. [S5]

narrative.text: Rep. Kathy Manning introduced the bill on November 9, 2023. [S5]
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced, and on November 10, 2023 to the Subcommittee on Health. [S5]
No further action was taken before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, so the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote. [S5]
The bill attracted one cosponsor, a fellow House Democrat, over its two-year life. [S4]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers who sponsor group plans keep their current cost-sharing arrangements, and patients with very high drug costs keep paying the full amount above current plan limits. No one gained directly; the bill simply cost nothing because it did nothing.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill capping monthly prescription drug cost-sharing at $250 per person. [S5]

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on November 9, 2023 and never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill. [S5]

sides.party_line_note: The only supporters were two House Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor); no Republican cosponsored, and the committee that controlled the bill was chaired by a Republican during this Congress. [S4] [S5]

industries.note: The bill caps what insurers can collect from patients for prescription drugs at $250 per person per month, forcing them to absorb charges above that level. Insurers would likely raise premiums on everyone to cover it, so the cost partly lands back on the public. [S3]
Group plans are bound by the same cap, so employers with generous drug coverage would face higher claims costs, some of which they may pass to workers through premiums or wages. [S3]

The cap does not touch drug prices. With patients insulated from costs above $250 a month, manufacturers can sustain high prices and the excess is paid through premiums rather than by the patient at the counter. [S3]
